title: Robust Quantum Memory Advantage from Contextuality
abstract: Quantum contextuality is widely recognized as an essential non-classical resource underlying quantum technology, yet illuminating the precise mechanisms through which it translates into unconditional computational advantages remains an ongoing challenge. We demonstrate an exponential, noise-resilient memory advantage for quantum finite automata arising from graph-theoretic approaches to contextuality. We define a promise problem on an exclusivity graph $G$ for which any classical deterministic automaton acts as a non-contextual hidden variable model requiring at least $N=χ(G)$ states, where $χ(G)$ is the graph's chromatic number. In contrast, by exploiting a structural phenomenon we term \textit{representational contextuality}, a QFA solves this task using a memory of dimension at most $d=ξ(G)+1$, where $ξ(G)$ is the graph's orthogonal rank. This separation scales exponentially ($d=\mathcal O(n)$ versus $N=2^{Ω(n)}$) for Boolean-orthogonality graphs. Crucially, this memory advantage maintains an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ threshold against both depolarizing and coherent noise.
summary: The paper establishes an exponential advantage for Quantum Finite Automata over classical automata by solving a problem rooted in contextuality. This advantage is quantified by the gap between the graph's chromatic number ($\chi$) and its orthogonal rank ($\xi$). Crucially, this resource separation remains robust even when subjected to realistic operational noise.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate an exponential, noise-resilient memory advantage for quantum finite automata (QFAs) over classical deterministic finite automata (DFAs) by exploiting graph-theoretic properties of contextuality.
main_result: An exponential separation is achieved in memory cost ($d=O(n)$ vs. $N=2^{\Omega(n)}$) when solving a promise problem derived from the Kochen-Specker Problem on Boolean-orthogonality graphs, and this advantage is robust to operational noise.
method: The analysis uses graph theory invariants ($\chi(G)$, $\xi(G)$) applied to an exclusivity graph $G$ to define a computational task. The quantum solution utilizes QFAs operating via Householder reflections, while the classical lower bound relies on the chromatic number.
model_or_system: The core model is the Quantum Finite Automaton (QFA) solving a promise problem defined by an exclusivity graph $G$. The underlying structure relates to the Kochen-Specker Problem and involves comparing the quantum memory dimension ($\xi(G)+1$) against the classical state requirement ($\chi(G)$).
key_observables: Chromatic number $\chi(G)$, orthogonal rank $\xi(G)$, Quantum Memory Dimension $d$, Classical State Requirement $N$.
important_parameters: The exponential separation scaling ($d=O(n)$ vs. $N=2^{\Omega(n)}$) for Boolean-orthogonality graphs, and the noise resilience threshold ($\mathcal{O}(1)$).
main_assumptions: The advantage relies on 'representational contextuality,' defined by the structural gap $\chi(G) > \xi(G)$, which is distinguished from statistical contextuality (SIC).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate graph structures like $\Omega_4$ and general graphs showing the relationship between $\chi$, $\xi$, and $\chi_f$. One figure compares linear quantum scaling to exponential classical lower bounds.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the computational problem (KSP on $G$), derives the classical lower bound using $\chi(G)$, proposes the QFA solution bounded by $\xi(G)+1$, proves the exponential separation, and finally distinguishes this 'representational' advantage from other forms of contextuality.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete computational realization of quantum resource theory, showing that structural incompatibilities between classical deterministic models (NCHVMs) and quantum mechanics can lead to provable, noise-resilient advantages in memory complexity for computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The complete Boolean-orthogonality graph Ω4. Vertices are colored such that no two connected vertices share a color, illustrating that χ(Ω4) = 4.

Figure 2: Scaling of the state space dimension as a function of the graph dimension n. While the quantum memory cost ξ(Ωn) (blue) grows linearly, the lower bound on the classical memory cost χ(Ωn) (red dashed), derived from the Frankl-Rodl (FR) theorem [35], grows exponentially.

Figure 3: This 18-vertex graph has χ = 7, ξ = 6 and χf = 5.68. It cannot exhibit state- independent contextuality because χf < ξ [18]. However, it does exhibit representational contextuality, as χ > ξ.

Figure 4: A valid 6-coloring of the 60-ray orthogonality graph of [42] derived from vertices of the 4D 600-cell. The graph is partitioned into 15 disjoint 4-element orthogonal bases (indicated by the shaded regions). Because each basis forms a clique, every region contains four distinct vertex colors.
